newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli bank to issue mortgage-backed securities.
newsitem.headline: Israeli bank to issue mortgage-backed securities.

text.p: Tefahot Israel Mortgage Bank plans to make a private placement of mortgage-backed securities and follow it with a public offering, Doron Nachmany, deputy managing director for planning, said on Tuesday.
"It will be a private issue, not public," Nachmany told Reuters. "We hope that during the course of the year we will be able to do a public offering."
The first issue, slated for early in 1997, will be sold to institutions, principally provident funds, although Nachmany said Tefahot hoped to interest other buyers.

He said the bank, Israel's largest home loan institution and a subsidiary of United Mizrahi Bank, hopes to raise 100-200 million shekels in the first issue, depending on how much the market can absorb.
Israel has no organised secondary mortgage market, so that Tefahot has taken on Meitav Investments and Securities as a financial adviser.

Nachmany said issuing mortgage-backed securities was aimed at addressing problems in obtaining financing. Tefahot and Israel's six other home loan banks get most of their funds from deposits made by institutions, mainly provident funds. However, most provident funds have reached the regulatory ceiling on mortgage bank deposits as a percentage of their portfolios, he said.
"When you do a transaction like this, you sell them the mortgages," Nachmany said. "It's not limited by the ceiling."
He said the securities would have a 15-20-year lifespan, but he refused to speculate on what their return would be.
"We have no experience with this, and the question is at what price we can sell them," he said.

Carmel Mortgage and Investment Bank made a small issue of mortgage-backed securities in 1989, but the market never developed. This month Finance Minister Dan Meridor appointed a Treasury committee to explore a secondary mortgage market and report back within 90 days.

Nachmany said he was sceptical that the government would succeed in creating the market. He said he could recall at least six such panels over the last few years, none of which saw its recommendations implemented.
"I don't think that in 1997 there will be a solution," he said.
